## Definition

The **mode** is the value that appears most frequently in a dataset. It is the only measure of central tendency that can be used with nominal (categorical) data.

## Characteristics

| Property | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| Frequency-based | Depends on count, not value |
| Any scale | Works with all measurement levels |
| May not exist | Possible when all values unique |
| May be multiple | Bimodal, multimodal distributions |

## Types of Modes

| Type | Description | Example |
|------|-------------|---------|
| Unimodal | One mode | 2, 3, **4**, **4**, **4**, 5, 6 |
| Bimodal | Two modes | **2**, **2**, 4, 5, **7**, **7** |
| Multimodal | Multiple modes | **1**, **1**, 3, **5**, **5**, **7**, **7** |
| No mode | All values unique | 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 |

## When to Use the Mode

The mode is most appropriate when:

- Data are categorical (nominal)
- Identifying the most common response
- Describing non-numeric data
- Identifying peaks in a distribution

## When Mode is Less Useful

- Continuous data with many unique values
- Small sample sizes
- When you need mathematical properties

## R Code Example

```r
# R doesn't have a built-in mode function
# Create your own
get_mode <- function(x) {
  uniq <- unique(x)
  uniq[which.max(tabulate(match(x, uniq)))]
}

get_mode(responses)

# Or use table to see frequencies
table(responses)
sort(table(responses), decreasing = TRUE)

# For multiple modes
get_modes <- function(x) {
  tab <- table(x)
  names(tab)[tab == max(tab)]
}
```

## Example: Categorical Data

Survey question: "What is your favourite research method?"

| Method | Count |
|--------|-------|
| Experiment | 45 |
| Survey | 32 |
| Interview | 18 |
| Observation | 5 |

**Mode**: Experiment (most frequently chosen)
